title: Scones
subtitle: Light, fluffy British scones for cream tea
excerpt: Classic British scones made with self-raising flour, butter, and buttermilk. Light and fluffy in the middle with a slight crust. Serve with clotted cream and jam for a proper cream tea.

recipe.sourceNotes: Scones are a British baking staple, central to the tradition of cream tea alongside clotted cream and jam. The Devon versus Cornwall debate about whether cream or jam goes on first is long-standing. The recipe is a simple rubbed-fat dough: cold butter rubbed into flour until the mixture resembles breadcrumbs, bound with buttermilk. Handling the dough as little as possible produces the lightest scones. Over-kneading develops the gluten and makes them tough.

content.text: Cold butter is essential: it must not melt into the flour during rubbing or the scones will be dense. Handle the dough as little as possible once the buttermilk is added. Cut the scones straight down without twisting the cutter: twisting seals the edges and prevents the scones from rising evenly.
Heat the oven to 220 C / fan 200 C / gas 7. Line a baking tray with baking paper.
Put the flour, salt, and butter into a large bowl. Rub the butter into the flour with your fingertips until the mixture resembles coarse breadcrumbs. Stir in the sugar.
Pour in the buttermilk. Mix quickly with a knife until the dough just comes together. It should be soft but not sticky. Do not knead.
Turn out onto a lightly floured surface. Pat to 2.5 cm thick. Cut out rounds with a 6 cm cutter, pressing straight down without twisting. Arrange on the tray. Re-roll the trimmings once to cut more.
Brush the tops with beaten egg. Bake for 10 to 12 minutes until risen and deep golden. Cool on a rack for at least 5 minutes before serving.
